Mutations are the only source of new alleles and occur continuously in living cells
Mutation rate increases when cells are exposed to mutagens such as radiation or certain chemicals
Sexual reproduction increases genetic variation through meiosis, chromosome shuffling and fertilisation
A population with more variation is better placed to survive environmental change

HIV spreads through body fluids and destroys T-helper lymphocytes, progressively weakening the immune system
HIV and AIDS are different: AIDS develops only when HIV has destroyed enough lymphocytes to collapse immunity
Antiretroviral drugs control HIV by stopping it replicating but do not cure the infection
Tobacco mosaic virus causes mosaic leaf patterns, reduces chlorophyll and lowers photosynthesis and crop yield
TMV spreads by contact and contaminated tools; infected plants cannot be cured and should be removed
Antibiotics do not work against viral diseases such as measles or HIV
TMV is spread by contact, not by insects, so mosquito nets do not help

points.label: Water is essential to life as a solvent, reactant, transport medium and for temperature regulation
The total amount of water on Earth is fixed and moves between stores in the water cycle
Evaporation and condensation are the key physical stage of the water cycle, driven by the Sun
Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from plant leaves through stomata, distinct from evaporation
Plants absorb water through root hair cells and transport it up through xylem to leaves
Animals return water to the environment through sweating, exhaling, urinating and defaecating
Precipitation includes rain, snow, sleet and hail; water then moves as runoff or soaks into groundwater
Deforestation reduces transpiration, lowering atmospheric water vapour and local rainfall

Human changes to land use (paving, drainage, irrigation, deforestation) alter how water moves through the cycle
Clouds are made of tiny liquid water droplets, not water vapour or gas
When sea water evaporates, dissolved salts are left behind, so rain is fresh water

Refraction occurs because wave speed changes at a boundary, bending the wave

Radio waves are produced by an oscillating current in an aerial at the same frequency
A radio wave absorbed by an aerial induces an alternating current at the same frequency
The ionosphere refracts radio waves back towards Earth, enabling long-range reception

Seismic waves refract and curve through Earth as speed changes with depth

Seismic surveying uses reflected waves from rock layers to locate oil and gas
Radar pulses measure glacier thickness; radio waves are absorbed by water so sound is used at sea
Both P-waves and S-waves are produced by earthquakes and detected by seismometers.
